results.content:
Loss guidance is a technique that minimizes the off-the-shelf loss function $L(X_0,y)$ during sampling:

$$\min_{X_0} L(X_0,y)$$
$$\text{s.t. } X_0 \in \mathcal{M}$$ (27)

where $y$ is the conditioning input, $\mathcal{M}$ denotes the conditional data manifold that follows the conditional distribution $p(X_0\mid\mathbf{C})$ learned by the diffusion model.
results.route_rationale: Statement of a constrained optimisation problem over an informally specified manifold; no crisp formal content.

fallback_result.reasoning:
Eq. (27) states a constrained minimisation, which is well-posed as written: an objective $L(X_0,y)$ and a feasible set $\mathcal{M}$. Nothing is derived from it in this snippet, so there is no step that could be algebraically invalid.

Two loosenesses, neither flagged. (i) The conditioning symbol switches mid-sentence: the objective is written $L(X_0, y)$ with "$y$ is the conditioning input", then the manifold is tied to $p(X_0\mid\mathbf{C})$ — $y$ and $\mathbf{C}$ are evidently the same object. (ii) Identifying the support of a learned distribution with a "manifold" is standard but informal in this literature, and no regularity is asserted that could be contradicted. No error.

results.location: B.1 Affordance Reasoning
results.content:
3D Object Point Cloud Encoding. We take as input a point cloud of an object, sampled to N points. The backbone is a ReCon++ [34] network (or a similar architecture) that processes these points and produces per-point feature representations
$$F_{\text{obj}} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times C},$$
which capture both local geometric details and the overall global context.

Multi-Token Fusion Mechanism. Rather than generating a single <AFF> segmentation token, PixelLM [36] defines, at each visual scale ℓ, a segmentation codebook comprising N learnable <AFF> tokens. After encoding the textual prompt, the model sequentially outputs the N tokens, each associated with a hidden vector $h_i^\ell$. A linear projection φ then aggregates these vectors into a unified representation
$$h^\ell = \phi(h_1^\ell, \ldots, h_N^\ell),$$
which is concatenated with the scale-specific image features and fed into the pixel decoder to produce the final segmentation mask. Experiments on the MUSE validation set indicate that increasing N from 1 to 3 improves cIoU.
results.route_rationale: Dimension declarations plus an aggregation map; the checkable content is symbol consistency, which is unformalisable.

fallback_result.reasoning:
The declarations are individually coherent: $F_{\text{obj}} \in \mathbb{R}^{N\times C}$ is the right shape for $N$ per-point features of width $C$, and $h^\ell = \phi(h_1^\ell,\ldots,h_N^\ell)$ is a well-formed aggregation of the per-token hidden vectors. No algebraic claim is made that could be false.

One genuine symbol collision, recorded but not flagged (this skill does not treat notation as an erratum-worthy error): $N$ denotes BOTH the number of point-cloud points in $F_{\text{obj}} \in \mathbb{R}^{N\times C}$ (thousands, since the clouds are described as upsampled then downsampled) and the number of learnable <AFF> tokens per visual scale in the codebook — which the same paragraph says is varied "from 1 to 3". So $h^\ell = \phi(h_1^\ell,\ldots,h_N^\ell)$ aggregates $N \in \{1,3\}$ vectors while $F_{\text{obj}}$ has $N \gg 3$ rows, and the two $N$'s cannot be the same integer. The prose makes the intent unambiguous, so no quantity is wrong. Also noted: the feature width $C$ is typographically close to the Interaction Prior $\mathbf{C}$ of Eq. (4), though the bold/plain distinction separates them.

results.location: B.2 Instruction Decomposition
results.content:
Instruction Text Encoding. We take a natural-language instruction $T_{\text{ins}}$ as the model input. The backbone is a LLaMA-style Transformer that produces token-wise hidden states $\{h_t\}_{t=1}^T$ and aggregates them via a pooling operation into a single embedding
$$h_{\text{cls}} \in \mathbb{R}^D,$$
which is then used for downstream tasks.

Boundary Localization & Hidden-State Extraction. Record the positions $t_1, \ldots, t_S$ where <AFF> appears. For each $i = 1, \ldots, S$, extract the corresponding last-layer hidden vector
$$z_i = h_{t_i} \in \mathbb{R}^D,$$
which encodes the full context immediately preceding the end of sub-task i.

Sequential Mask Decoding. For each step i, use the query E_i to perform cross-attention over the point features F_obj and decode a per-point mask:

M_i(p) = σ(Decoder(\tilde{F}_p, z_i)) for p = 1, …, N,

where \tilde{F} are the fused features and σ is the sigmoid activation.

The mathematical content is sound as far as it goes: $z_i = h_{t_i} \in \mathbb{R}^D$ is a well-typed selection of $S$ hidden vectors at the recorded <AFF> positions $t_1,\ldots,t_S$, and $M_i(p) = \sigma(\mathrm{Decoder}(\tilde{F}_p, z_i))$ for $p = 1,\ldots,N$ correctly yields a per-point mask value in $(0,1)$ for each of the $N$ points, since $\sigma$ is the sigmoid. There is no derivation here, hence no invalid step.

Three presentation defects, recorded but not flagged as errors: (i) the text says "use the query $E_i$ to perform cross-attention", but $E_i$ is never defined anywhere in the manuscript and does not appear in the formula, which uses $z_i$ instead — a dangling symbol; (ii) $\tilde{F}$ ("the fused features") is introduced only in the `where` clause with no definition relating it to $F_{\text{obj}}$; (iii) $T$ is reused for the instruction's token count in $\{h_t\}_{t=1}^T$ while elsewhere denoting the diffusion horizon ($T = 1000$), and the index base is $1$-based here against Eq. results.location: C.6 Ablation Study on Motion In-between Refinement
results.content:
Motion In-between Metric. To the best of our knowledge, no previous work has defined an evaluation metric for motion in-between hand-object interaction. We thus introduce a simple yet effective measure, the “Smooth Rate,” to quantify the temporal continuity of interpolated motion segments as follows:

SmoothRate = dFID/dt, (28)

where dt is the derivative of time. The results are shown in Table A8 and Table A9.
results.route_rationale: A definition that asserts a quantity is well-defined and computable; the assertion is checkable but rests on undefined objects, so it is unformalisable.

fallback_result.reasoning:
Eq. (28) does not define a computable quantity, yet three tables of results (A8, A9, A10) are reported in its units.

1. $\mathrm{FID}$ is a distributional statistic — a Fréchet distance between the Gaussian moments of two SETS of motion features. It is a functional of a whole collection of sequences, not a function of a scalar time variable, so the derivative $d\mathrm{FID}/dt$ has no referent: there is no differentiable map $t \mapsto \mathrm{FID}(t)$ in the paper to differentiate. §4.2 confirms this reading, defining FID as computed "between real and synthesized motions in a pre-trained motion feature space".

2. The gloss "where $dt$ is the derivative of time" is not a definition and is self-contradictory: $dt$ is a differential, not a derivative, and calling it "the derivative of time" explains nothing. Read charitably as "$dt$ is the time increment", the expression becomes a finite difference $\Delta\mathrm{FID}/\Delta t$ — but then neither the increment $\Delta t$ (in frames? seconds?) nor the windows over which the two FIDs are computed is specified, so the metric is still not reproducible.

3. Table A10 settles that a finite-difference estimator with free parameters is in fact being used: it sweeps a "window size" over $\{1,3,5,10,20\}$ and reports materially different SmoothRates ($4.77$ down to $2.98$ on GRAB-seen). That window is a parameter of the estimator Eq. (28) does not describe, so Eq. (28) is strictly weaker than what was computed.

This matters because SmoothRate is introduced as a NEW metric ("no previous work has defined an evaluation metric for motion in-between") and is the sole basis for the motion-in-between ablations — where it carries large claimed effects ($38.18 \to 2.98$ on GRAB, $41.37 \to 6.77$ on ARCTIC). As stated, those numbers cannot be reproduced or checked. Severity minor: the metric is confined to §C.6 and does not enter the main results of Tables 2/3.

fallback_result.reasoning:
First, what IS correct: the counting claim holds. Of the $10 \times 4 = 40$ entries in Table A11, exactly four exceed $0.05$ — FOL (Unseen) $3.0\times10^{-1}$, and Diversity (Seen) $1.5\times10^{-1}$, $1.0\times10^{-1}$, $1.4\times10^{-1}$ — so $36/40$ are $\le 0.05$ and "the majority of metrics" is arithmetically supported. I confirmed this entry by entry.

The error is in the inference rule, not the count. "[R]epeating each test five times and reporting the mean p-value" does not yield a p-value: the arithmetic mean of several p-values is not itself a valid p-value and has no calibrated interpretation at a $0.05$ threshold. Under the null, $p \sim \mathrm{U}(0,1)$ has mean $1/2$, and the mean of $k$ independent nulls concentrates at $1/2$ with standard deviation $1/\sqrt{12k}$ — it is not uniform, so thresholding it at $0.05$ does not control the Type-I error rate at $5\%$. It is anti-conservative as used here; the standard valid bound (Rüger / Vovk-Wang) is that $2\bar{p}$, not $\bar{p}$, is a conservative p-value, and the standard valid combiners are Fisher's method or Stouffer's Z. So the conclusion "significant at the 95% confidence level ... (p-value $\le 0.05$)" does not follow from the tabulated quantities, whatever their values. Compounding it, no multiple-comparison correction is applied across the 40 simultaneous tests, yet the per-test $0.05$ threshold is read as a global claim.

Two corroborating internal contradictions. (ii) The significance claim sits against §4.4's own characterisation of the same ablations as "minor degradations", "small semantic misalignments" and "incremental", and §4.3's statement that "differences are within standard deviations reported by prior works".

findings.evidence:
Lean proved that the sampling step of Eq. (8) is inconsistent with the posterior the paper derives itself in Eqs. (25)-(26), for **every** admissible noise-schedule value.

Eq. (8) writes $X_{t-1} = \mu_t + \sigma_t\varepsilon$ with $\varepsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)$, so the step's variance is $\sigma_t^2$. Eq. (25) gives that posterior variance as $\tilde{\beta}_t = \frac{(1-\alpha_t)(1-\bar{\alpha}_{t-1})}{1-\bar{\alpha}_t}$, so consistency demands $\sigma_t = \sqrt{\tilde{\beta}_t}$. The paper instead sets $\sigma_t = \frac{1-\bar{\alpha}_{t-1}}{1-\bar{\alpha}_t}\beta_t$, which `sigmaEq8_eq_postVar` proves is identically $\tilde{\beta}_t$ itself — the **variance**, not its square root.

`eq8_variance_never_matches` then compiles: since `postVar_mem_Ioo` establishes $0 < \tilde{\beta}_t < 1$ for all $0<\alpha_t<1$, $0<\bar{\alpha}_{t-1}<1$, we get $\tilde{\beta}_t^2 < \tilde{\beta}_t$, hence $\sigma_t^2 \ne \tilde{\beta}_t$ everywhere on the admissible domain — a general refutation, not an isolated counterexample. Witness (`eq8_variance_witness`): at $\alpha_t = \bar{\alpha}_{t-1} = \tfrac12$ the posterior variance is $\tfrac13$ but Eq. (8) samples with variance $\tfrac19$. Taken literally the reverse process is under-dispersed by a factor $\sqrt{\tilde{\beta}_t} < 1$ at every timestep.

The mean is fine: `mean_matches` confirms Eq. (8)'s $\mu_t$ equals the Eq. (26) posterior mean exactly, once $\beta_t = 1 - \alpha_t$ is substituted. The defect is isolated to the $\sigma_t$ definition.

This cannot be dismissed as a typesetting artifact, because the paper's **own** Eq. (14) uses the same symbol with the opposite convention: `eq8_eq14_incompatible` proves $\sqrt{d\,\sigma_t} \ne \sqrt{d}\,\sigma_t$ for all $\sigma_t > 0$, $\sigma_t \ne 1$, so Eq. (14) is correct only if $\sigma_t$ is a variance while Eq. (8) is correct only if it is a standard deviation. Severity is minor because Eqs. (25)-(26) state the variance correctly and the empirical results do not depend on this transcription.

Eq. (12) is presented as "the analytical solution to enforce steepest gradient descent" under the Spherical Gaussian Constraint, but Lean proves the vector it writes does not satisfy that constraint.

The genuine analytic solution, formalised and proved in a real inner-product space, is the **normalised** gradient: `norm_of_true_solution` and `steepest_descent_on_sphere` compile, showing $D = -\dfrac{r}{\|g\|}g$ lies on the sphere $\|D\| = r$ and minimises the linearised loss change $\langle g, D\rangle$ over it (minimum $-r\|g\|$, by Cauchy-Schwarz), where $g = \nabla_{X_t} l$.

Eq. (12) omits the $1/\|\nabla l\|$ factor. `eq12_off_the_sphere` compiles: $\|-r\,g\| = r\|g\| \ne r$ whenever $\|g\| \ne 1$. Its norm is $r\|\nabla l\|$ — off by the full gradient magnitude. Witness (`eq12_witness`): with $\|\nabla l\| = 5$ and radius $r = 1$, the stated direction has norm $5$, not $1$.

The proof deliberately leaves the radius as an arbitrary $r > 0$, so the refutation holds under **either** reading of the paper's $\sqrt{d\sigma_t}$ typesetting and does not depend on resolving that ambiguity.

Consequence: $D^\star$ enters only via $D_{\text{mix}} = D_{\text{sample}} + w(D^\star - D_{\text{sample}})$, which Eq. (14) renormalises, so the radius error is absorbed downstream — but not harmlessly. The mixture weighting between the descent and stochastic directions then scales with $\|\nabla l\|$, making the effective guidance strength drift with gradient magnitude rather than holding at the intended $w$. Severity minor: the DSG construction being cited is itself correct, so this reads as a dropped normalisation in transcription.

The same $\sigma_t$ defect as Eq. (8), recurring at a second site — and here Lean also confirms the surrounding algebra is right, which isolates the error precisely.

Correct part: `eq20_weight_is_coef_sq` compiles, proving the bracketed weight $\dfrac{\bar{\alpha}_{t-1}(1-\alpha_t)^2}{(1-\bar{\alpha}_t)^2}$ is exactly the square of the Eq. (25) posterior-mean coefficient of $X_0$, namely $\dfrac{\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_{t-1}}(1-\alpha_t)}{1-\bar{\alpha}_t}$ — which is what the Gaussian-KL substitution $\mathrm{KL} = \|\mu_q-\mu_\theta\|^2/(2\sigma_t^2)$ produces. The weight matches the standard $x_0$-prediction objective.

Refuted part: the prefactor $\dfrac{1}{2\sigma_t^2}$ requires $\sigma_t^2$ to **be** the posterior variance, but the definition supplied immediately below sets $\sigma_t$ equal to that variance. `eq20_sigma_never_matches` compiles: $\sigma_t^2 \ne \tilde{\beta}_t$ for every admissible $0<\alpha_t<1$, $0<\bar{\alpha}_{t-1}<1$, because $0 < \tilde{\beta}_t < 1$ there. The prefactor is therefore off by a factor of $\tilde{\beta}_t$.

Severity minor: the very next sentence discards this prefactor ("After removing constant terms"), so the loss actually optimised — Eq. (21) — is unaffected. This is the same root cause as the Eq. (8) finding ($\sigma_t$ defined as a variance, used as a standard deviation) and a single corrected definition fixes both sites.

Eq. (28) does not define a computable quantity, yet Tables A8, A9 and A10 report results in its units.

1. **The derivative has no referent.** $\mathrm{FID}$ is a distributional statistic — a Fréchet distance between the Gaussian moments of two **sets** of motion features ( §4.2: "between real and synthesized motions in a pre-trained motion feature space"). It is a functional of a whole collection of sequences, not a function of a scalar time variable, so there is no differentiable map $t \mapsto \mathrm{FID}(t)$ in the paper for $d\mathrm{FID}/dt$ to differentiate.

2. **The gloss defines nothing.** "[W]here $dt$ is the derivative of time" is self-contradictory: $dt$ is a differential, not a derivative. Read charitably as "$dt$ is the time increment", Eq. (28) becomes a finite difference $\Delta\mathrm{FID}/\Delta t$ — but neither the increment (frames? seconds?) nor the windows over which the two FIDs are computed is given, so the metric remains unreproducible. The defect survives the charitable reading, so it is not a typo.

3. **Table A10 confirms hidden estimator parameters.** It sweeps a "window size" over $\{1,3,5,10,20\}$ and reports materially different SmoothRates ($4.77 \to 2.98$ on GRAB-seen). That window is a parameter of the estimator actually used, which Eq. (28) does not mention — so what was computed is strictly richer than what was defined.

This matters because SmoothRate is introduced as a **new** metric ("no previous work has defined an evaluation metric for motion in-between hand-object interaction") and is the sole basis for the motion-in-between ablations, where it carries large claimed effects ($38.18 \to 2.98$ on GRAB, $41.37 \to 6.77$ on ARCTIC). As stated, those numbers cannot be reproduced or checked. Severity minor: the metric is confined to §C.6 and does not enter the main results of Tables 2/3.

As printed, the penetration loss cannot do what it is introduced to do — its minimiser maximises contact rather than preventing penetration.

Eq. (10) is an **unsigned** squared Euclidean distance between hand vertices and the closest affordance region. It is non-negative and attains its global minimum, zero, exactly when the hand vertices **coincide** with the object points. Minimising it therefore pulls hand vertices onto, and with no barrier to stop them through, the object surface — the opposite of "mitigat[ing] interpenetration artifacts" and of the refinement objective the paper lists as "physical constraint refinement to prevent penetration".

A loss that penalises penetration must be sensitive to the **sign** of the hand-object relation, e.g. a signed-distance hinge $\sum_v \max\big(0, -\mathrm{SDF}_{\text{obj}}(v)\big)^2$, which vanishes for every vertex outside the object and grows only as vertices move inside it. Eq. (10) carries no sign and no hinge.

Corroboration that this is a real mismatch rather than a misreading: Eq. (10) is structurally **identical** to the affordance-**attraction** loss of Eq. (9) — same indicator gating, same squared distance to the "closest affordance region" — with only $\hat{J}$ (joints) replaced by $\hat{V}$ (vertices) and the superscript `joint` by `vert`. Two losses the paper presents as serving opposite geometric purposes are given the same attracting functional form, so at most one of the two stated purposes can be served.

Severity minor: Tables 4/5 show a measurable effect from removing $l_{\text{penetration}}$ and Table A3 reports improved interpenetration volume (IV), so the implemented loss evidently differs from the printed one. The defect is in the formula as stated, not in the empirical results. It does, however, touch the abstract's promise of "a training-free physics refinement stage that minimizes penetration", so an erratum restating the loss is warranted.

The stated domain constraint on the guidance scale is violated by the paper's own sensitivity analysis.

Eq. (22) asserts $s \geq 1$. Tables A5/A6 sweep the guidance parameter over $\{0.5, 2.0, 2.5, 3.0, 5.0\}$, which includes $s = 0.5 < 1$.

The identification is not a guess. Appendix A reports "a guidance scale of 2.5"; Tables A5/A6 include a $2.5$ row; and that row reproduces the Table 2 "Ours" GRAB-seen numbers digit for digit — $47.64{\pm}1.03$, $0.26{\pm}0.02$, $26.43{\pm}0.77$, $3.69{\pm}0.27$, $24.59{\pm}2.01$. So the quantity swept in Tables A5/A6 is the one Appendix A sets to $2.5$, i.e. the guidance scale $s$ of Eq. (22), and the sweep breaches the printed constraint.

Compounding this, "guidance rate" — the heading of Tables A5/A6 — is also the name Eq. (13) gives to a **different** parameter, the mixing weight $w$ in $D_{\text{mix}} = D_{\text{sample}} + w(D^\star - D_{\text{sample}})$. Under that alternative reading the tables would report $w \in \{2.0, 2.5, 3.0, 5.0\}$, far outside the $[0,1]$ range in which Eq. (13) is a convex interpolation between the stochastic and descent directions. Either way a stated constraint is violated, so the two parameters are conflated somewhere in §C.4.

Severity minor: classifier-free guidance is well-defined for $0 \le s < 1$ (it interpolates toward the unconditional prediction instead of extrapolating), so the remedy is to relax the printed constraint and disambiguate the two names, not to redo any experiment. Confidence is held at $0.72$ because it rests on the terminology collision resolving the way the matching numbers indicate.

The significance claim is drawn through an invalid combination rule, so it does not follow from the tabulated numbers.

First, what checks out: the **counting** claim is right. Of the $10\times 4 = 40$ entries in Table A11, exactly four exceed $0.05$ — FOL (Unseen) $3.0\times10^{-1}$, and Diversity (Seen) $1.5\times10^{-1}$, $1.0\times10^{-1}$, $1.4\times10^{-1}$ — so $36/40$ are $\le 0.05$ and "the majority of metrics" is arithmetically supported.

The error is the inference rule. "[R]epeating each test five times and reporting the mean p-value" does not produce a p-value: the arithmetic mean of several p-values is not itself a valid p-value and has no calibrated interpretation against a $0.05$ threshold. Under the null, $p \sim \mathrm{U}(0,1)$ has mean $\tfrac12$, and the mean of $k$ independent nulls concentrates at $\tfrac12$ with standard deviation $1/\sqrt{12k}$ — it is not uniform, so thresholding $\bar{p}$ at $0.05$ does not control the Type-I error rate at $5\%$, and is anti-conservative as used here. The standard valid bound (Rüger / Vovk-Wang) is that $2\bar{p}$, not $\bar{p}$, is a conservative p-value; the standard valid combiners are Fisher's method or Stouffer's $Z$. No multiple-comparison correction is applied across the 40 simultaneous tests either, yet the per-test threshold is read as a global claim.

Two corroborating internal contradictions: the table is captioned "Two-test Statistically Insignificant" while the section is "Statistical Significance" and the text claims significance — the caption asserts the opposite of what it labels; and the claim sits against §4.4's own description of the same ablations as "minor degradations", "small semantic misalignments" and "incremental", and §4.3's "differences are within standard deviations reported by prior works".

Severity minor: Tables 4/5 report the ablation effect sizes independently, so the paper's conclusions do not rest solely on §C.9. Also noted: the last two columns share the identical header "w/o l", leaving it indeterminate which refers to $l_{\text{penetration}}$ and which to $l_{\text{aff}}$.

summary:
Mathematical verification of **OpenHOI** (open-world hand-object interaction synthesis). Extracted **24** self-contained mathematical objects — every display equation in §3.1-3.2 and Appendices B.1-B.4, the two multi-step derivation chains, three definitional blocks and one inferential claim about the ablation statistics. **7** were routed to `verify-math-lean` for formal proof and **17** to informal `verify-math` review. The Lean arm settled all 7: **4 PASSED, 3 REFUTED, 0 FAILED**, so no informal fallbacks were needed and no snippet was left unsettled.

### What Lean proved correct
The paper's diffusion mathematics is, in its substance, right. Four machine-checked proofs, all `sorry`-free on standard Mathlib axioms:
- **Eq. (5)/(15), forward marginal** — $p(X_t|X_0) = \mathcal{N}(\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_t}X_0, (1-\bar{\alpha}_t)I)$ follows by induction from the per-step kernel and $\bar{\alpha}_t = \prod_{i=1}^t\alpha_i$ (`forward_variance`, `forward_mean`).
- **Eqs. (16)-(19), the ELBO** — the load-bearing step (18)→(19) is Jensen's inequality for $\log$, and the direction is correct; proved from $\log x \le x-1$ rather than by citing a library lemma (`jensen_log`, `elbo_direction`).
- **Eqs. (23)-(26), the reverse posterior** — the completing-the-square step (24)→(25) is exact, including the delicate part: the full exponent identity holds for every $x$ **with no residual constant**, confirming the $q(X_t|X_0)$ denominator cancels cleanly. Both the stated mean and variance are right (`precision_matches`, `mean_matches`, `complete_the_square`).
- **Eq. (14), the DSG constraint radius** — $\sqrt{d\,\sigma_t} = \sqrt{d}\sqrt{\sigma_t}$ is exactly the correct spherical-Gaussian radius $\sqrt{d}\,\sigma_{\text{std}}$, *given* that the paper's $\sigma_t$ is a variance (`eq14_radius_correct`).
Lean also independently confirmed two sub-parts of otherwise-flagged equations: Eq. (8)'s mean $\mu_t$ matches the posterior mean exactly, and Eq. (20)'s bracketed weight is exactly the square of the Eq. (25) $X_0$-coefficient, as the Gaussian-KL substitution requires.

### What Lean refuted
All three refutations are compiling proofs of the negation, not stalled proof searches, and **all three trace to two dropped factors in transcription** rather than to any flaw in the underlying derivations:
1. **One root cause, two sites — $\sigma_t$ is a variance used as a standard deviation.** Eq. (8) samples $X_{t-1} = \mu_t + \sigma_t\varepsilon$, so its variance is $\sigma_t^2$; but $\sigma_t$ is defined as $\frac{1-\bar{\alpha}_{t-1}}{1-\bar{\alpha}_t}\beta_t$, which Lean proves is identically the posterior variance $\tilde{\beta}_t$ of Eq. (25) — so the square root is missing. Because $0 < \tilde{\beta}_t < 1$ throughout the admissible domain, $\sigma_t^2 \ne \tilde{\beta}_t$ *everywhere*, not just at isolated points. Eq. (20) repeats the same definition under a $1/(2\sigma_t^2)$ prefactor, inheriting the same defect.
2. **Eq. (12) is missing the gradient normalisation.** Presented as "the analytical solution" of steepest descent under the Spherical Gaussian Constraint, it writes $D^\star = -r\nabla l$ instead of $-r\,\nabla l/\|\nabla l\|$, so its norm is $r\|\nabla l\|$ and it does not lie on the sphere it is the solution for. The proof fixes an arbitrary radius $r>0$, so this verdict is independent of whether the paper's $\sqrt{d\sigma_t}$ means $\sqrt{d\sigma_t}$ or $\sqrt{d}\,\sigma_t$.

**No verifier disagreement arose** — every Lean verdict was PASSED or REFUTED, so no claim rested on an informal second opinion, and no finding rests on a Lean failure.

A note on how the two arms reinforced each other: the Eq. (14) PASS is what makes the Eq. (8) refutation airtight. Eq. (14) is correct **only** under the variance reading of $\sigma_t$, while Eq. (8) is correct **only** under the standard-deviation reading, and `eq8_eq14_incompatible` proves no single reading satisfies both. So the $\sigma_t$ problem cannot be waved away as a markdown-extraction artifact of $\sqrt{d\sigma_t}$ versus $\sqrt{d}\sigma_t$.

### What informal review added
Four further findings, none formalisable:
- **Eq. (10), the penetration loss** does the opposite of what it is introduced for. It is an *unsigned* squared distance, minimised at zero when hand vertices coincide with the object — so minimising it drives vertices *into* the surface. It is also structurally identical to the affordance-*attraction* loss Eq. (9) (joints→vertices), so at most one of the two opposite stated purposes can be served. Preventing penetration requires a signed-distance hinge. The ablations show $l_{\text{penetration}}$ does help and Table A3 reports improved IV, so the implemented loss evidently differs from the printed one.
- **Eq. (22)'s $s \geq 1$** is breached by the paper's own sweep over $\{0.5, 2.0, 2.5, 3.0, 5.0\}$. The identification is pinned down by the $2.5$ row of Table A5 reproducing the Table 2 "Ours" GRAB-seen numbers digit for digit, matching Appendix A's "guidance scale of 2.5". "Guidance rate" is moreover used for both $s$ and the Eq. (13) mixing weight $w$.
- **Eq. (28), SmoothRate $= d\mathrm{FID}/dt$**, is not a computable quantity: FID is a set-level distributional statistic, not a differentiable function of time, and "$dt$ is the derivative of time" defines nothing. Table A10's sweep over "window size" $\{1,3,5,10,20\}$ confirms a finite-difference estimator with parameters Eq. (28) never states. This newly-introduced metric is the sole basis for Tables A8-A10.
- **§C.9's significance claim** reports "the mean p-value" over five repetitions, which is not a valid p-value and does not control Type-I error at the $0.05$ threshold (the valid bound is $2\bar{p}$; valid combiners are Fisher or Stouffer), with no correction across 40 simultaneous tests. The *counting* claim itself checks out: exactly 4 of 40 entries exceed $0.05$, so "the majority" is accurate. Table A11 is also captioned "Two-test Statistically **Insignificant**" while asserting significance.

### Verdict
**MINOR_ERRORS.** Seven confident findings, all `minor`: none invalidates a main claim. The core derivations — forward process, ELBO, reverse posterior — are formally verified correct, and the two refuted transcription defects ($\sigma_t$ missing a square root; Eq. (12) missing $1/\|\nabla l\|$) are each repaired by a one-symbol correction that leaves the surrounding mathematics, and the empirical results, intact. Notably the $\sigma_t$ defect is confined to the definition: the loss actually optimised (Eq. 21) discards the affected prefactor, and Eqs. (25)-(26) state the variance correctly. Verdict confidence is high ($0.85$) because it rests on four machine-checked PASSes and three machine-checked REFUTATIONs covering every non-trivial equation in the paper, with zero unsettled Lean runs.

### Out of scope — flagged for other verifiers
Per this skill's extraction rules, numeric experimental results were not extracted as snippets, but two inconsistencies surfaced while reading and are worth routing to `verify-vision` / `verify-consistency`: (i) Table 5 reports ARCTIC-seen "Ours" as FID $19.74{\pm}0.35$ and Diversity $2.65{\pm}0.16$, whereas Table 3 and Table A6 both give $19.74{\pm}0.16$ and $2.65{\pm}0.03$ for the same configuration — the two standard deviations appear transposed in Table 5; (ii) Table 5's "w/o CFG" ARCTIC-seen Diversity is $3.39{\pm}0.18$, exactly the ARCTIC **GT** Diversity value, while every other ARCTIC Diversity entry lies in $[1.5, 2.7]$, suggesting a copied cell. Separately, the manuscript's equation numbering skips **(3)**, leaving "where the weights $\lambda_{\text{task}}, \lambda_{\text{aff}}$ are utilized to balance the different loss items" dangling with no equation defining the combined MLLM objective.
